headline: New Haven Breakwall on the Dying Ebb: Porgies Stacked, Sea Bass Sneaking In
subhead: Bunker schools are pulling stripers and bluefish tight to Charles Island while the rockpiles keep grinding out porgies and blackfish.
body_markdown:
Tuesday evening, last two hours of the ebb, I'm working the outer arm of the New Haven breakwall with a high-low rig baited with green crab, and I've got a porgy pinning the rod tip down before the sinker even settles. Nine and a half inches, fat as a softball. Two drops later, another one just as good. That's the rhythm right now on the rockpiles — not fast, but honest, and the size class has crept up noticeably from where it sat back in July.

We flagged this last week — said the porgy bite would stay the most dependable structure fishing in this stretch while the bluefish push spread east from the Western Sound reefs, and that's exactly the shape of it right now. Porgies are thick on the breakwalls, the Merwin Point riprap, and the rockier stretches off Sandy Point, biting best on the last two hours of an outgoing tide when the current slows enough for them to leave the bottom clutter and feed in the open. Sandworm and green crab are both producing, though on calmer evenings I'll switch to squid strips because the porgies seem less picky about presentation when the water's laying down flat.

Sea bass are mixed in with the porgies on the same drops, which is the tell that the water's still carrying decent warmth — Kings Point read just under 71 the other day, and while I don't have a hard number off New Haven, the bite behavior says we're running close to that. Sea bass want a little more structure than porgies, so I've been picking through them tighter to the rock edges, dropping skimmer clam on a bucktail teaser above the hook. Nothing giant — mostly a foot to fourteen inches — but steady enough that if you're patient and willing to move a rod length here and there along the wall, you can put together a nice mixed bag without much trouble.

Blackfish are the wildcard. I made a few short drifts off Stratford Shoal and Falkner Island this week with green crabs on knocker rigs, and while I got a couple of teaser bites, the real tog bite hasn't kicked in yet — water's still a touch warm for them to commit the way they will once September cools things down. I wouldn't write the season off, but right now I'd call blackfish a bonus fish, not a target.

The bigger story, and the one every angler on this stretch is talking about at the dock, is the bunker. Peanut schools have been thick off Charles Island and along the bar that runs south off the point, and stripers are working them hard on the tide change — I watched three separate blitzes from the beach at Silver Sands over the weekend, gulls diving, bass busting bunker right up on the sandbar in three to six feet of water. That kind of visible mid-August surface activity is a little unusual for this time of year, and it lines up with what we called last week about the new moon tides sharpening the bite at current-driven structure. The stronger push around the August 12 moon has kept bait moving and concentrated tight to the bar, and the bass have been happy to follow it in.

The pattern that's worked for me: fish the last hour of the flood into the top of the high, casting bunker spoons and white paddle-tail swimbaits right into the edge of the bait balls off Charles Island. If the fish are busting on top, a topwater walk-the-dog bait will draw strikes, but once the blitz goes subsurface — which it usually does within twenty minutes — I switch to a bunker chunk fished on a fish-finder rig just off the sandbar drop where the water goes from three feet to twelve. Most of what's coming over the rail is slot-sized, twenty-four to thirty inches, with the occasional bigger fish mixed in chasing the same bait. Bluefish are riding shotgun in these same schools, and they're not shy — if you're using anything with hooks exposed, expect some leader damage. I've had good luck avoiding the worst of it with a short length of 40-pound fluorocarbon ahead of the lure.

Hammonasset and the Milford Gulf have been quieter by comparison — I made a pass through the Gulf on Thursday morning and found bait but not much committed feeding, which tells me the fish are still concentrating tighter around Charles Island and the harbor mouth rather than spreading evenly across the whole beat. Worth checking again if the bunker schools push east, but for now I'd put my time where the birds are working.

Looking ahead, I don't see any reason for this pattern to break in the next week. The tide's still building strong off the new moon, bait's staying put, and the warm push through the Western and Central Sound isn't showing signs of backing off. If the wind stays out of the south and doesn't kick up a chop on the bar, I'd fish the flood at Charles Island for bass and bluefish, then finish the day on the breakwall for porgies and sea bass as the tide drains out. That's the one-two I'm planning to run again this weekend, and it's about as reliable a combination as this stretch offers in mid-August.
